tips.title: Multiply for the total, count for the wanted
tips.body: The number of outcomes is the product: a 4-sided spinner and a coin give $4 \times 2 = 8$. Then **count** the outcomes you want. Never estimate the count.

tips.title: Pairs are equally likely, totals are not
tips.body: With two dice, the 36 **pairs** are equally likely but the 11 **totals** are not: 7 happens six ways and 12 only once. Always work in the grid of pairs, then group.

tips.title: The counts must add to the total
tips.body: Add up how many outcomes fall in each category. If they do not come to the total number of cells, an outcome has been missed, and that is the commonest error in the topic.

tips.title: Count the grid, do not reason about it
tips.body: Once the grid is drawn, **count** the outcomes you want and **count** the total. Counting is reliable where reasoning about totals is not, which is exactly why two dice feel misleading: the pairs are equally likely and the totals are not.

why.matters:
A sample space diagram is the most honest tool in probability: write down every outcome, then count the ones you want. No formula, no cleverness, no way to fool yourself.

Its real value is that it shows you **which outcomes are equally likely and which are not**. That distinction is where most wrong answers in probability come from, and a grid makes it impossible to miss.

examples.title: Why board games are built around 7
examples.body:
Roll two dice and add them. The totals run from 2 to 12, but they are not equally likely, and the grid shows why in one glance.

There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Only 1 of them makes 2, and only 1 makes 12. But 6 of them make 7, because 7 can be built 6 different ways. So 7 is 6 times as likely as 2.

That is not a curiosity, it is the design of the games. Settlers of Catan marks 6 and 8 as its best-yielding numbers — the two nearest 7 — and then makes 7 itself the robber, so the likeliest roll is the one that costs you. In Monopoly the orange properties are the most landed on, because they sit 6 to 9 steps past Jail and Jail is where players most often begin a turn.

A designer who assumed the totals were equally likely would produce a board nobody wanted to play twice.

visual.alt: A six by six grid of the totals from two dice, showing that seven appears six times down the leading diagonal while two and twelve appear only once each in opposite corners

steps.title: Listing every outcome, once each
steps.body:
When two things happen together, a **sample space diagram** lists every outcome that could result. Edexcel also calls it a **possibility space**.

It matters because probability from a list only works if the list is **complete** and every outcome in it is **equally likely**. Then

$$P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{number of outcomes in the event}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$$

The diagram does the hard part: it stops you missing outcomes and it stops you counting any twice. Almost every lost mark in this topic is a missing outcome, not a wrong division.

visuals.alt: Four boxes about sample space diagrams: what a sample space is, why one is drawn, what it needs to be valid, and the probability formula it gives

check.prompt: Why does a sample space diagram have to list every possible outcome?
check.solution: The total number of outcomes is the **denominator**. Miss one and every probability you read off the diagram is wrong.
options: The mean of the outcomes cannot be found without it
It makes the diagram easier to draw and to label
A missing outcome makes the denominator wrong
Otherwise the outcomes stop being equally likely

steps.title: A spinner and a coin
steps.body:
A fair spinner numbered **1 to 4** is spun and a fair coin is flipped. Each spinner number can pair with each coin side, so the grid has $4 \times 2 = 8$ cells.

The grid is the whole method: build it, then count.

visuals.alt: A sample space grid for a four-sided spinner and a coin, with the spinner number down the side and heads or tails across the top, giving eight outcomes

visuals.problem: Find the probability of an even number and a head

steps.text: The grid holds **8** outcomes, and they are equally likely
The even numbers are 2 and 4, so the outcomes wanted are **2H** and **4H**
steps.note: read them off the grid, do not imagine them

steps.text: That is **2** outcomes out of 8

check.prompt: A fair spinner numbered 1 to 4 is spun and a fair coin is flipped. What is the probability of a 3 and a tail? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
check.solution: There are $4 \times 2 = 8$ outcomes and only one of them is 3T, so $P = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$.

steps.title: Two dice, and a grid of sums
steps.body:
When the question asks about the **total**, put the total in each cell rather than the pair. Here are two fair four-sided dice, so the grid has $4 \times 4 = 16$ cells.

With the sums written in, every question becomes counting cells.

visuals.alt: A sample space grid of the totals from two four-sided dice, with the first die down the side and the second across the top, giving sixteen totals
A table of how many of the sixteen totals take each value from 2 to 8

visuals.problem: Find the probability that the total is at least 6

steps.text: Totals of 6, 7 and 8 are the ones wanted
From the table: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ways
steps.note: count the cells, do not guess

steps.text: Check: the counts in the table add to 16, the whole sample space
steps.note: if they do not, an outcome is missing

check.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 5? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
check.solution: Four of the sixteen cells give a total of 5, so $P = \dfrac{4}{16} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.

steps.title: The outcomes have to add up to 1
steps.body:
Two rules from the specification are worth stating plainly, because they give you a free check and sometimes a free answer.

- The probabilities of an **exhaustive** set of outcomes, meaning a set that covers everything that can happen, **sum to 1**.
- The probabilities of an exhaustive set of **mutually exclusive** events, meaning events that cannot both happen, also **sum to 1**.

So if a question gives you all but one probability, the missing one is $1$ minus the rest. And whenever you finish a sample space question, add the counts: they must come to the total number of outcomes.

The same idea gives the **complement**: $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$. When an event is awkward to count and its opposite is easy, count the opposite and subtract. "At least one" is nearly always easier as $1 - P(\text{none})$.

visuals.alt: A table showing the probabilities of three colours in a bag of twenty counters adding up to one

visuals.problem: A bag holds red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 0.25 and P(blue) = 0.4. Find P(green)

steps.text: The three colours are exhaustive: one of them must be drawn

check.prompt: A bag holds only red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 0.15 and P(blue) = 0.45. Work out P(green).
check.solution: The three are exhaustive, so they sum to 1: $P(\text{green}) = 1 - 0.15 - 0.45 = 0.4$.

steps.title: When a list beats a grid
steps.body:
A grid works for exactly **two** things happening. For three or more, or when the two things have different kinds of outcome, write a **systematic list** instead.

Systematic means in an order you can defend, so you can see nothing is missing. Fix the first item, run through all the seconds, then move the first on by one.

visuals.problem: List every outcome when a coin is flipped three times

steps.text: Fix the first flip as H, then list the rest in order: **HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT**
Now fix the first flip as T: **THH, THT, TTH, TTT**
steps.note: four more, in the same order

steps.text: That is $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ outcomes, which matches the list
Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH, so **3** outcomes
$P(\text{exactly two heads}) = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$

check.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of getting three tails? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
check.solution: There are $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ equally likely outcomes and only TTT gives three tails, so $P = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$.

steps.title: Your turn: build the grid, then read it
steps.body:
A fair four-sided die numbered 1 to 4 is thrown and a fair coin is flipped.

1. Draw the sample space grid. How many outcomes should it have before you start?
2. Find $P(\text{an odd number and a head})$.
3. Find $P(\text{not a 4})$, using the complement rather than counting.

Then change the die to a six-sided one and say what happens to the total number of outcomes, and why.

props.title: Fill this in first, then count

visuals.alt: A blank sample space grid for a four-sided die and a coin, with the die numbers down the side and heads and tails across the top

check.prompt: A fair four-sided die numbered 1 to 4 is thrown and a fair coin is flipped. What is the probability of an odd number and a head? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
check.solution: The grid has $4 \times 2 = 8$ outcomes. The odd numbers are 1 and 3, so 1H and 3H are wanted: $\dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.

steps.title: Going deeper: when the outcomes are not equally likely
steps.body:
The formula $\dfrac{\text{wanted}}{\text{total}}$ is only valid when the outcomes are **equally likely**. Top marks go to students who notice when they are not.

Take the **total** of two dice. There are 11 possible totals, 2 to 12, but $P(\text{total} = 7)$ is not $\dfrac{1}{11}$. The **totals** are not equally likely; the **pairs** are. Seven happens six ways and two happens only one way.

So always count in the sample space of **equally likely** things, which is the pairs, and then group them. That is exactly what the grid does, and it is why the grid is worth drawing even when you think you can do it in your head.

The same trap appears with a biased spinner or a bag whose counters are not in equal numbers. There, count **counters**, not **colours**.

props.title: Eleven totals, but not one eleventh each

visuals.alt: A table showing that the eleven totals of two ordinary dice are not equally likely, giving the number of ways each total can happen out of thirty-six

steps.text: There are 11 totals, so $\dfrac{1}{11}$ looks tempting
steps.note: this is the trap the question is set for

steps.text: But the **totals** are not equally likely: 7 happens 6 ways and 12 happens 1 way
steps.note: count in the grid, not in the list of totals

steps.text: The **pairs** are equally likely, and there are $6 \times 6 = 36$
steps.note: this is the correct sample space

steps.text: $P(\text{total} = 7) = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}$
Check: the 11 counts add to 36, so no pair has been missed

check.prompt: A student says the probability that two dice total 7 is one eleventh, because there are 11 possible totals. What is wrong?
check.solution: The **pairs** are equally likely, not the totals. Seven happens six ways out of 36 and twelve only once, so the sample space must be the 36 pairs.

options: The two dice are not independent of each other
The probability should be out of 6 rather than 11
The totals are not all equally likely
There are twelve possible totals, not eleven

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **sample space diagram**, or possibility space, lists every outcome of two things happening together.
- Use a **grid** for two things, and a **systematic list** for three or more.
- $P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{outcomes in the event}}{\text{total outcomes}}$, but **only** when the outcomes are equally likely.
- The total number of outcomes is the product: 4 spinner results and 2 coin results give $4 \times 2 = 8$.
- The probabilities of an **exhaustive** set of outcomes **sum to 1**, so a missing one is $1$ minus the rest.
- $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$. Count the opposite whenever it is easier.
- The **totals** of two dice are not equally likely. Count in the grid of pairs, then group.
- Always check the counts add back to the total. A missing outcome is the commonest error in this topic.

rows: three or more, or unlike outcomes
multiply the number of results for each
outcomes in the event ÷ total outcomes
the counts add back to the total

questions.prompt: A fair spinner numbered 1 to 4 is spun and a fair coin is flipped. How many outcomes are there altogether?
questions.solution: Each of the 4 spinner results pairs with each of the 2 coin results: $4 \times 2 = 8$.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are thrown and the totals are recorded. How many cells does the sample space grid have?
A bag holds only red, blue and yellow counters. P(red) = 0.3 and P(blue) = 0.5. Work out P(yellow).
questions.solution: The three colours are exhaustive, so $P(\text{yellow}) = 1 - 0.3 - 0.5 = 0.2$.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for two events to be mutually exclusive?
questions.solution: **Mutually exclusive** events cannot both happen. If they are also exhaustive, their probabilities sum to 1.
options: They cover every possible outcome
One happening makes the other more likely
They are equally likely
They cannot both happen

questions.prompt: A fair four-sided die and a fair coin are used. What is the probability of a 2 and a head? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: There are $4 \times 2 = 8$ equally likely outcomes and one of them is 2H, so $P = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is even? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: The even totals are 2, 4, 6 and 8, happening $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8$ ways out of 16, so $P = \dfrac{8}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of exactly two heads? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: The 8 outcomes are HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. Three of them have exactly two heads, so $P = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$.

questions.prompt: A sample space grid is drawn for two events and the counts in it add to 15, but the grid should have 16 cells. What has gone wrong?
questions.solution: The counts must add to the total number of cells. Fifteen against sixteen means **an outcome has been missed**.
options: The probabilities do not sum to 1
An outcome has been missed
One outcome has been counted twice
The outcomes are not equally likely

questions.prompt: P(it rains tomorrow) = 0.35. What is the probability that it does not rain tomorrow?
Why is a systematic list better than writing outcomes down as they occur to you?
questions.solution: Working in a fixed order lets you **see** that the list is complete. Outcomes written down at random are how outcomes get missed.

markScheme.description: an order shows nothing is missing

options: It makes the outcomes equally likely
An order you can defend shows nothing has been missed
It is quicker to write
It avoids having to count the total

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are thrown. What is the probability of a double? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: The doubles are (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) and (4,4), so 4 cells out of 16: $P = \dfrac{4}{16} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is at least 6? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: Totals of 6, 7 and 8 happen $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$ ways out of 16, so $P = \dfrac{6}{16} = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$. Note that 'at least 6' includes 6.

questions.prompt: Two ordinary six-sided dice are thrown. Why is the probability of a total of 7 not one eleventh?
questions.solution: The **pairs** are equally likely, not the totals. A total of 7 happens 6 ways out of 36 while 12 happens once, so $P = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.

markScheme.description: the totals are not equally likely

options: The dice are not independent
A total of 7 is impossible
The eleven totals are not equally likely
There are twelve totals, not eleven

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of at least one head? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: 'At least one head' is everything except TTT. $P(\text{no heads}) = \dfrac{1}{8}$, so $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{7}{8} = 0.875$.

markScheme.description: uses the complement, or lists the 7 outcomes

questions.prompt: A four-sided spinner is biased. P(1) = 0.2, P(2) = 0.35 and P(3) = 0.15. Work out P(4).
questions.solution: The four outcomes are exhaustive, so they sum to 1: $P(4) = 1 - 0.2 - 0.35 - 0.15 = 0.3$.

markScheme.description: subtracts the three given probabilities from 1

questions.prompt: A fair four-sided die numbered 1 to 4 is thrown and a fair coin is flipped. Draw the sample space diagram and use it to find the probability of an even number and a tail.
questions.solution: The sample space is a grid with the four die numbers down the side and heads and tails across the top, giving eight outcomes: 1H, 1T, 2H, 2T, 3H, 3T, 4H and 4T. These eight are equally likely because both the die and the coin are fair. The even numbers are 2 and 4, so the outcomes wanted are 2T and 4T, which is two of the eight. The probability is therefore two eighths, which cancels to one quarter, or 0.25.

markScheme.description: a grid or list with all 8 outcomes
identifies 2T and 4T as the outcomes wanted

criteria.text: Draws a grid or systematic list showing all eight outcomes
Identifies 2T and 4T as the outcomes wanted
Writes the probability as 2 out of 8

questions.modelAnswer:
**The sample space.** Put the die numbers down the side and the coin across the top:

| Die | Heads | Tails |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1H | 1T |
| 2 | 2H | 2T |
| 3 | 3H | 3T |
| 4 | 4H | 4T |

That is $4 \times 2 = 8$ outcomes, and they are **equally likely** because both the die and the coin are fair.

**Reading it.** The even numbers are 2 and 4, so the outcomes wanted are **2T** and **4T**: two of the eight.

$$P = \dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$$

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice numbered 1 to 4 are thrown and the totals are recorded. Explain why the probability of a total of 4 is not one seventh, and find the correct probability.
questions.solution: There are seven possible totals, running from 2 up to 8, which is why one seventh looks tempting. But the totals are not equally likely, so they cannot be used as the sample space. A total of 2 can only happen one way, as 1 and 1, whereas a total of 5 can happen four ways. The things that are equally likely are the pairs, and there are four times four, which is sixteen of them. A total of 4 comes from the pairs 1 and 3, 2 and 2, and 3 and 1, which is three pairs. The probability is therefore three sixteenths, or 0.1875.

markScheme.description: states that the totals are not equally likely
identifies the 16 pairs as the correct sample space
finds the 3 pairs giving a total of 4

criteria.text: Explains that the seven totals are not equally likely
Identifies the 16 equally likely pairs as the sample space
Finds the three pairs that give a total of 4

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why one seventh is wrong.** The totals run from 2 to 8, so there are seven of them, which is where $\dfrac{1}{7}$ comes from. But the **totals are not equally likely**, so they cannot be the sample space. A total of 2 happens only one way, as $1 + 1$, while a total of 5 happens four ways.

**The correct sample space** is the **pairs**, which *are* equally likely. There are $4 \times 4 = 16$ of them.

**Counting.** A total of 4 comes from $(1,3)$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,1)$: **three** pairs.

$$P(\text{total} = 4) = \dfrac{3}{16} = 0.1875$$

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped four times. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.solution: Each flip has 2 results and there are 4 flips: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^4 = 16$.

examTechnique.body:
Draw the grid every time, even when the numbers look easy enough to hold in your head. Every year students lose marks trying to keep two dice straight without one, and it takes twenty seconds.

Write the **totals** in the cells when the question is about totals, and the **pairs** when it is about the pair. Deciding which before you start saves redrawing it.

Count, then check. The counts in your grid must add back to the total number of cells. That single check catches the missing outcome, which is the most common error in this topic.

Cancel your fraction. A probability left as $\dfrac{6}{36}$ will usually still score, but $\dfrac{1}{6}$ is what the mark scheme prints and it costs nothing.

Watch for 'at least'. **At least 6** includes 6. **More than 6** does not. And when 'at least one' appears, reach for $1 - P(\text{none})$ before you start listing.
examinerErrors: Missing an outcome, so the denominator is wrong and every answer with it.
Treating the totals of two dice as equally likely. The pairs are equally likely; the totals are not.
Reading 'at least 6' as 'more than 6', which loses the cells where the total is exactly 6.
Counting (1,3) and (3,1) as the same outcome. On two separate dice they are different cells.
Giving the answer as a ratio, such as 3:16. A probability is a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
Leaving the fraction uncancelled when the mark scheme wants it in its simplest form.
Forgetting that an exhaustive set sums to 1, and so working the long way round a missing probability.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer draws the sample space even when the numbers look easy, and says in words that the outcomes are equally likely before dividing. It knows the difference between the grid of pairs and the list of totals, and can explain why a total of 7 is not one eleventh. It uses the complement when the opposite event is easier to count, writes 'at least' inclusively, checks that the counts add back to the total, and cancels the final fraction.
